result.markdown: --- course-unit: a07-surrogate-models status: complete --- # Surrogate and emulator models An epidemic simulator can be accurate and still be too expensive to call inside an uncertainty analysis, calibration loop, or optimal-design calculation. A **surrogate** (or emulator) is a cheaper function fitted to simulator outputs. It is not a replacement for the mechanistic model: its predictions are useful only over a declared input domain and should be accompanied by an error assessment. ## Learning goals By the end of this appendix you should be able to: - distinguish a simulator, a training design, and a surrogate prediction; - use the current `Surrogates.jl` 7 interface to fit a radial-basis emulator; - measure out-of-sample error rather than judging a surrogate only by its training fit; and - identify when a response surface is a poor summary of an epidemic model. ## Model assumptions and classification We use the homogeneous baseline SIR model from the course. It is a deterministic, continuous-time, continuous-state, population-level model. A single scalar input, the per-contact transmission probability `β`, varies while the contact rate `c = 10.0` and recovery rate `γ = 0.25` remain fixed. The population is `N = 1000`, with `(S(0), I(0), R(0)) = (990, 10, 0)`. The surrogate is therefore a deterministic map from one parameter to one quantity of interest, not a stochastic epidemic model. We choose the recovered fraction at a finite horizon, `t_f = 40`, as the quantity of interest. In a larger application the same workflow could emulate peak prevalence, an observation likelihood, or an intervention cost. The training design has only twelve points, deliberately making the approximation error visible while keeping this example CI-sized. ## Equations Let `ρ = βc` be the effective transmission rate. The simulator solves $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm dS}{\mathrm dt} &= -\rho\frac{SI}{N},& \frac{\mathrm dI}{\mathrm dt} &= \rho\frac{SI}{N}-\gamma I,& \frac{\mathrm dR}{\mathrm dt} &= \gamma I. \end{aligned} \tag{1} $$ {#eq-a07-sir} For a selected value of `β`, the target supplied to the surrogate is $$ q(\beta) = \frac{R(t_f;\beta)}{N}. \tag{2} $$ {#eq-a07-target} The fitted function `\widehat q(\beta)` is an approximation to `q(β)`. We evaluate it at parameter values that were not used for fitting and calculate $$ e_j = \widehat q(\beta_j) - q(\beta_j),\qquad \operatorname{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}e_j^2}. \tag{3} $$ {#eq-a07-error} In the code, `sir_ode!` implements the three derivatives in @eq-a07-sir, `final_recovered_fraction` implements @eq-a07-target, and `RadialBasis` represents `\widehat q`. ## Julia implementation ### Simulator and training design The shared course module supplies the baseline state, parameter type, and right-hand side. `Surrogates.sample` with `LatinHypercubeSample()` gives one stratified point per interval in this one-dimensional design. The seed makes the displayed training design reproducible. ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using CairoMakie using EpiModelingCourse using OrdinaryDiffEq using Random using Statistics using Surrogates const a07_u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0] const a07_tspan = (0.0, 40.0) const a07_lb, a07_ub = 0.02, 0.08 function final_recovered_fraction(β) parameters = SIRParameters( beta = β, contact_rate = 10.0, gamma = 0.25, N = 1000.0, ) problem = ODEProblem(sir_ode!, a07_u0, a07_tspan, parameters) solution = solve( problem, Tsit5(); saveat = [a07_tspan[2]], abstol = 1e-9, reltol = 1e-9, ) return solution[3, end] / parameters.N end Random.seed!(20260711) n_train = 12 β_train = sample(n_train, a07_lb, a07_ub, LatinHypercubeSample()) y_train = final_recovered_fraction.(β_train) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 12-element Vector{Float64}: 0.8071519990309515 0.9131875581901288 0.9317587984202617 0.7370855561687782 0.6296326847876723 0.888458193036905 0.8547262984673037 0.1247720041417495 0.94595053567218 0.4681467063823326 0.056632999018633515 0.27222390982984446 ``` ::: ::: ### Current `Surrogates.jl` API `Surrogates.jl` 7 uses callable surrogate objects. The radial-basis constructor takes locations, responses, lower and upper bounds, and a radial function. The explicit `cubicRadial()` call is intentional: it is the current constructor form, rather than the zero-argument-free function used in some older examples. We qualify `update!` because plotting packages can export unrelated methods with the same name. ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} surrogate = RadialBasis( β_train, y_train, a07_lb, a07_ub; rad = cubicRadial(), ) β_test = collect(range(a07_lb, a07_ub; length = 64)) y_test = final_recovered_fraction.(β_test) y_pred = surrogate.(β_test) errors = y_pred .- y_test validation_summary = ( rmse = sqrt(mean(errors .^ 2)), max_abs_error = maximum(abs.(errors)), training_points = length(β_train), ) validation_summary ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (rmse = 0.005079064991333957, max_abs_error = 0.030386676263557774, training_points = 12) ``` ::: ::: The surrogate is also incrementally extensible through `update!`. This is useful when validation identifies a region that needs another expensive simulator run; it is not a substitute for retaining a held-out validation set. ::: {#6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} β_new = 0.051 Surrogates.update!(surrogate, β_new, final_recovered_fraction(β_new)) surrogate(β_new) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 0.7890325067446844 ``` ::: ::: ### Visualizing the approximation and its error The left panel compares the mechanistic simulator on a dense grid with the surrogate. The right panel is the important diagnostic: it shows absolute error at held-out values. The figure is produced by CairoMakie from the values calculated above, not by manually copying computed numbers. ::: {#cell-fig-a07-surrogate-error .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig = Figure(size = (900, 400)) ax1 = Axis( fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Transmission probability β", ylabel = "Recovered fraction at t = 40", ) lines!(ax1, β_test, y_test; color = :black, linewidth = 3, label = "SIR simulator") lines!(ax1, β_test, y_pred; color = :darkorange, linewidth = 2, label = "Surrogate") scatter!( ax1, β_train, y_train; color = :steelblue, markersize = 9, label = "Training points", ) axislegend(ax1; position = :lt) ax2 = Axis( fig[1, 2], xlabel = "Transmission probability β", ylabel = "|surrogate − simulator|", ) scatter!(ax2, β_test, abs.(errors); color = :firebrick, markersize = 7) hlines!(ax2, [0.01]; color = :gray, linestyle = :dash, label = "1% error") axislegend(ax2; position = :lt) fig ``` ::: {#fig-a07-surrogate-error .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` A radial-basis emulator of the finite-horizon recovered fraction, with held-out absolute error. ::: ::: For a high-dimensional input, replace the scalar `β` values by vectors and use vector lower and upper bounds. The same callable interface remains, but the training design must cover a much larger space. ## Validation The validation cell reports error on the 64-point grid, including points that are not training locations. A small maximum error in this example is evidence about this domain and this target only. It does not establish accuracy for a different horizon, a different initial condition, or a two-parameter `(β, γ)` design. We also check the simulator itself: the SIR total `S + I + R` is conserved up to the numerical tolerance used by `OrdinaryDiffEq`. ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} β_check = 0.053 check_parameters = SIRParameters(beta = β_check, contact_rate = 10.0, gamma = 0.25, N = 1000.0) check_solution = solve( ODEProblem(sir_ode!, a07_u0, a07_tspan, check_parameters), Tsit5(); saveat = 0.25, abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10, ) population_error = maximum(abs.(sum(Array(check_solution); dims = 1)[:] .- check_parameters.N)) (; validation_summary, population_error) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (validation_summary = (rmse = 0.005079064991333957, max_abs_error = 0.030386676263557774, training_points = 12), population_error = 5.684341886080801e-13) ``` ::: ::: ## Interpretation and limitations The emulator is valuable when each ODE solve is expensive and many predictions are needed. It can support screening, visualization, or a proposal mechanism before a final decision is checked against the simulator. The error plot makes the validation claim appropriately modest: it describes interpolation over the specified `β` interval. Radial-basis interpolation can extrapolate badly outside `[a07_lb, a07_ub]` and can be sensitive to clustered or poorly scaled inputs. Twelve points are not enough for a serious multi-parameter epidemic analysis. A surrogate can also smooth a threshold, miss a narrow peak, or hide solver failures if the training pipeline records only a scalar output. Preserve the original model, use a separate validation design, and re-simulate any policy or scientific conclusion with the mechanistic model. See the maintained [Surrogates.jl radial-basis documentation](https://docs.sciml.ai/Surrogates/stable/radials/) and its [surrogate interface reference](https://docs.sciml.ai/Surrogates/stable/surrogate/). ## Exercises ### Exercise 1 {#a07-ex1} Extend the emulator to two inputs, `β` and `γ`, over `β ∈ [0.02, 0.08]` and `γ ∈ [0.15, 0.35]`, while keeping `c`, `N`, and the initial state fixed. Use at least 24 Latin-hypercube training points and a separate 5 × 5 validation grid. Report the RMSE and maximum absolute error, and explain where the two-dimensional surrogate is least accurate. ### Exercise 2 {#a07-ex2} Replace the smooth recovered fraction with the discontinuous-looking target `max(I(t)) / N` over `t ∈ [0, 40]`. Use the same training and validation design, plot the absolute error, and compare it with the error for `R(40) / N`. Explain why a response involving an internal maximum can require more training points even though the underlying ODE is smooth. ## Companion materials - [Slides](../slides/appendices/07-surrogate-models.html) - [Pluto preview](../notebook-exports/appendices/07-surrogate-models.html) - [Pluto source](../notebooks/appendices/07-surrogate-models.jl)
